newsitem.title: USA: Thompson still believes China role in U.S. election.
newsitem.headline: Thompson still believes China role in U.S. election.

text.p: Sen. Fred Thompson admitted Saturday he could only build a circumstantial case that China tried to influence the 1996 U.S. elections because the key players had refused to testify or fled the United States.
But he said he stood by his belief that the Chinese had such a plan.

When in July he launched the Senate's hearings on campaign fund-raising scandals, Thompson, a Tennessee Republican, said there was a Chinese plan to influence the outcome of U.S. presidential and congressional elections.

But he has presented little concrete evidence to substantiate that view, although the panel has heard testimony from people who wrote checks to the Democratic National Committee on behalf of foreigners.
One of the key Democratic fund-raisers with ties to China, John Huang, said he would only testify if he was protected from prosecution.

"We've got all of these connections that millions of dollars of foreign money (were) coming in here with (Huang's) intermediaries, all of whom have unlimited access to the White House apparently," Thompson said in an interview on CNN's "Evans and Novak" programme.

"And in every case they've either left the country (or) taken the Fifth Amendment," he said. "We're getting no cooperation from the government of China. So we're having to build a circumstantial evidence case."
But Thompson refuted comments by others that he was backing down on the China plot. "In terms of the plan itself, the existence of the plan, there's no question about that."
Thompson said Huang had dropped out of sight, after offering to testify as long as he was given immunity.
"But our door is open if they've got credible information to give to us, but we're not going to give him a blank check and a 'get out of jail' card just based on some vague promises," Thompson said.

The Tennessee senator attacked the White House for holding back evidence. Last week an Asian tycoon testified that he had given the Democratic Party hundreds of thousands of dollars, and a day later administration officials disclosed that he had visited the White House several times between 1994 and 1996.

"I can only conclude that they're deliberately delaying the production of documents," Thompson said on Saturday, adding that he believed the president should show more outrage about the fund-raising revelations.
"We're seeing things unfold here that's got to be troubling to any American citizen, especially any sitting president," he said.
